author: brian-carroll
body:
The empty string literal was originally intended to have a binary representation of "all zeros", with a null pointer and zero length.

But that means it doesn't have the "small string flag" set, like other strings below a certain size. So the flag status for string literals is:

| Length                | Small string bit |
| --------------------- | ---------------- |
| 0                     | 0                |
| 1 to (2 * PTR_SIZE - 1) | 1                |
| >= 2 * PTR_SIZE       | 0                |

But in the Str library (in both Rust and Zig), when we create a new string, we do a check like `length < 2*PTR_SIZE` to decide whether to make it a small string or not. There's no special case for zero length! So if the length happens to be zero, then we get an empty string whose "small string flag" is set.

That gives us an ambiguity - we have two different representations for the empty string. And to deal with the ambiguity, we had lots of checks like `str.isSmallStr() || str.isEmpty()`. (And the `isEmpty()` method itself had two branches, for "big" and "small" empty strings.)

This logic is more complicated than it needs to be, and seems bug-prone. In fact we had various places that *should* have been checking for `str.isSmallStr() || str.isEmpty()`, but weren't.

In a [Zulip thread](https://roc.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/231635-compiler-development/topic/Are.20empty.20strings.20small.3F) we decided that this is more hassle than it's worth. Having the "all zeros" representation for the empty string isn't getting us much benefit to compensate for the more complicated logic.

The new simpler truth table is as below
| Length                | Small string bit |
| --------------------- | ---------------- |
| 0 to (2 * PTR_SIZE - 1) | 1                |
| >= 2 * PTR_SIZE       | 0                |

We create strings in the following places. The "all zeros" version of empty string has been removed from each one, so it can't exist anymore.
- Zig builtins Str library `RocStr.allocate()`
- Rust Str library `RocStr::default()` and `RocStr::from_slice_with_capacity_str()`
- String literals in each of the backends

linux-gen: random: improve ODP_RANDOM_BASIC data and random test data

    odp_random_test_data() and _odp_random_std_data() (used when OpenSSL
    random is not enabled).
    
    Signed-off-by: Jere Leppänen <jere.leppanen@nokia.com>

validation: random: add test for buffer overflow and alignment problems
    
    Add a new test, which checks that odp_random_data() and
    odp_random_test_data() do not modify bytes outside the given buffer.
    
    Signed-off-by: Jere Leppänen <jere.leppanen@nokia.com>
    Reviewed-by: Petri Savolainen <petri.savolainen@nokia.com>

validation: random: test randomness
    
    Test that random data looks random by adding four new tests:
    
    random_test_frequency checks that random data is uniformly
    distributed.
    
    random_test_independence checks that bytes are independent.
    
    random_test_runs checks that the number of runs (uninterrupted
    sequence of identical bits) is what is expected of random data.
    
    random_test_matrix_rank checks that the ranks of 32x32 binary matrices
    correspond to expected probabilities.
    
    Signed-off-by: Jere Leppänen <jere.leppanen@nokia.com>
```

author: rolfbjarne
body:
Once upon a time there was a single VTCompressionSession.Create method, which
was [driving users insane][1] - they had to manually call CFRetain to avoid
crashes! What an abomination!!

Insane users are clearly not happy users, and we wanted happy users, so time
and effort went into creating a solution: a new Create overload was devised
and [implemented][1], taking extreme care to not break our brave and insane
existing users who had to manually call CFRetain. Because the fix would break
existing users - the now extraneous CFRetain would mean that their apps would
leak memory. *A lot* of it! That's bad, so we decided to make sure that didn't
happen.

Of course, dear old Murhpy wanted a say, so the new Create overload didn't do
as intended. In fact, it had the same insane behavior the old Create overload
had! Ops.

But Murphy decided to have even more fun: the changes were so buggy, that they
in fact fixed the old Create overload! Which from now on wouldn't require the
horrendous manual CFRetain calls... and effectively introducing the leak the
fix was trying so hard to not introduce.

Oh dear Murphy.

Of course he had another trick up his sleeve: in our extreme efforts to help
our users, we added an Obsolete attribute that would tell people to use the
new Create overload.

Let that sink in for a moment: we had an Obsolete attribute on a function that
was (now) perfectly fine, telling users to use a function that was broken.

To get the correct behavior, users would now have to to remove their manual
CFRetain calls, and ignore the obsolete warning on the old (and correct)
Create overload which told users to use the new (and buggy) Create overload.

In other words: still insanity, just a slightly different flavor.

Murphy had a field day!

Time went by, and eventually a sane enough user [reported the insanity to
us][2]. Even better: the user actually provided a fix! Truly, we have some
amazing users.

Unfortunately, the user didn't have access to our code history, and thus was
obviously not able to see the whole picture, and the fix ended up being
incorrect.

Unrelated lesson learned: don't forget your history, otherwise you'll end up
repeating mistakes from the past.

So now came the problem: how to fix all the APIs? In a way that didn't make
our users' existing apps just suddenly start crashing or leaking?

There really was no way, so nothing really happened for quite a while.

Then, an opportunity presented itself: we'd be able to do [widespread breaking
changes][3].

So, hoping that Murphy stays away this sunny winter day, I'm changing both the
new and the old Create overloads to do the right thing. But only in .NET,
where we can do breaking changes! Or at least that's my intention. I've tried
to stave off our dear old friend by adding his arch enemy: unit tests. Which,
of course, Murphy couldn't stay away from, but it seems adding a few
Thread.Sleep calls makes him bored enough to stay away. Hopefully for good...

[1]: https://github.com/xamarin/maccore/commit/66c50b9a176c6edfa8e633bfd9b54831ebddc9e5
[2]: https://github.com/xamarin/xamarin-macios/pull/2070
[3]: https://github.com/xamarin/xamarin-macios/issues/13087

author: petercrocker
body:
Suggested changes:

two cumulus j2 templates are missing do write at the end, causing two issues:

changes aren't saved, only left as running config in vtysh, so don't get reflected in cumulus net show commands
if you configure both OSPF and BGP module settings, the second config.sh file overwrites the first, resulting in only one of two modules being configured
sort ansible.cfg settings, which will make it easier to add/diff them when they change in the future

add 'ansible_managed = # Ansible Managed File' to ansible.cfg. This allows you to put {{ ansible_managed }} in the top of any j2 template, making it clear to someone looking at the resulting templated file that it's auto-generated by ansible, not user-editable. this setting doesn't harm anything in netsim_tools, but makes it easier to extend.

add 'filter_plugins = ./filter_plugins' to ansible.cfg. I use an arista-provided filter plugin (aka an ansible filter like "| ipaddr" ) called natural_sort which properly sorts numbers like 010 before 11. this setting doesn't harm anything in netsim_tools, but makes it easier to extend.

change 'roles_path=./roles' so that i can add ansible roles in the roles/ directory instead of cluttering up the root netsim-tools folder. this setting doesn't harm anything in netsim_tools, but makes it easier to extend.

change default libvirt mem for cumulus image from 768m to 1024m. In the past, 768 was enough for the last 5 years, but it's just at a tipping point where certain more complex configs will exhaust the memory.

change default libvirt mem for linux image from 512m to 1024m. If you want to do any kind of testing on the linux boxes and install packages, you can quickly run out of memory.

As a related point, maybe it would be better to expose the VM default settings as user-configurable, as opposed to being compiled in to the python package? For example, netlab allows the -defaults option, but this doesn't expose VM settings.

change bridge name in vagrant-libvirt.xml to be virbr9, instead of vibr2. Less likely to collide with an existing bridge on a user's system (which it does on mine!)

correct MAC addresses on lines 22-23 of vagrant-libvirt.xml. Ivan you need to work on your hex counting ;) it's 08, 09, 0A not 08, 09, 10! The result is the ansible playbooks using the hosts.yml file created won't connect to the vms if they get those bad mac addresses.

added more MAC addresses to the vagrant-libvirt.xml. Otherwise a user can create a sim with a limit of about 10 devices.

added a section to the docs on bgp.originate, because a working example is always better, and I had to figure it out, incorrectly the first time.

author: andrewpochapsky
body:
Every message that previously accepted a `name: String` now accepts `name: Option<String>`. This allows users who only want to store a single primitive to do so without needing to pick a name. Under the hood, if no name is specified, the primitive is given a default key.

The keys have also been made globally unique to make it easier for other contracts to interact with it (they no longer need to provide the key creator's address to the query). Now only the creator of the contract can modify the key values.

author: bamieh
body:
## Summary

### Fix `bulkFetch` logic

Fixed a bug where we used to call every collector's `fetch` function regardless if they've returned `true` or `false` in their `isReady` function. Updated `bulkFetch` logic to only collect from ready collectors.

Collectors that take longer than the `maximumWaitTimeForAllCollectorsInS` configuration will be considered as not ready and skipped from the collection.

The config  `maximumWaitTimeForAllCollectorsInS` default value is now equal to 4seconds. This should be more than enough time for the collector to return a value from `isReady`.

### Remove `areAllCollectorsReady` function

Our external API expects people to call `areAllCollectorsReady` first then `bulkFetch`.

The function `areAllCollectorsReady` was useless as its logic is no longer relevant after we've removed telemetry from monitoring. This is what the `areAllCollectorsReady` used to do:

1. Calls the `isReady` function for every collector.
2. if some collectors return `isReady: false` then the function will always return `true` regardless after the first 60 seconds have passed since the first time `areAllCollectorsReady` was called.
3. This means that this function will only return `false` to block collecting usage during the first 60 seconds after Kibana starts.

This function was implemented this way because:
1. The collectors were part of `monitoring`. Monitoring starts collecting stats as soon as the plugin's start is called. This logic gives plugins 60seconds at the startup of kibana to be ready before ignoring their `isReady` completely.
2. On the next attempt to fetch telemetry the `collectorSet` recalculates how much time is left from the 60s and then if the 60s is over it starts returning `true` regardless if all of the collectors are ready or not.
3. In the past Monitoring used to loop over the collectors every 10seconds so this will fail 6 times if some collectors are not ready, then starts trying to fetch regardless after that.


This function is only used in 2 places and the reason it was needed in the first place is no longer valid.
1. The `stats` api: currently the stats api is broken because of the existing logic.
2. Server-side fetcher: we already wait 5 minutes on Kibana startup time.

We want to send the data of the ready collectors on request even if some collectors are not ready. Currently if some collectors are not ready we block sending the stats and since we no longer have very frequent polling this could hurt us when attempting to send from the server-side for example.

### Fix stats API broken on M1 machines

Updating the `bulkFetch` logic to accommodate for errors and timeouts in `isReady` function automatically resolves this issue. 

The stats API was broken due to the Reporting plugin failing to start due to an unsupported platform: `darwin-arm64` (mac m1 chip) which causes the reporting collector's `isReady` function to hang indefinitely waiting for the plugin to `start`. 

To resolve the core issue in reporting I've opened a ticket for the team to follow up: _issue TBD_

Closes https://github.com/elastic/kibana/issues/119477

## Description
The QT GUI Frequency Sink block segfaults if a large (e.g. 8192) or small (e.g. 17) FFT size is specified, and the Control Panel is subsequently opened. This happens because there are no bounds checks on the index computed here:
https://github.com/gnuradio/gnuradio/blob/19864fc6ede818b169259607bb85bd5931013e02/gr-qtgui/lib/freqcontrolpanel.cc#L243-L247

It looks like this bug has been around since the control panel was added in https://github.com/gnuradio/gnuradio/pull/459, so GNU Radio 3.7.7+ would be affected.

## Which blocks/areas does this affect?
* QT GUI Frequency Sink

I used this flow graph to test:
![Screenshot from 2021-12-16 13-11-17](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/583749/146426015-ce18d513-01d9-4db3-b135-631e2476e0cc.png)
After starting the flow graph, middle click on the Frequency Sink and click "Control Panel". Prior to this change, a segfault will occur. Same if the FFT size is changed to 17.

**Context:**
This PR fixes the following codefactor issues that seem to be appearing for the first time [here](https://github.com/PennyLaneAI/pennylane/pull/1973/files).

1. Line 205 in pennylane/templates/layers/cv_neural_net.py is missing `do_queue` argument which leads to an `arguments-differ` issue.

2. Line 149 in pennylane/templates/subroutines/qpe.py is missing `do_queue` argument which leads to an `arguments-differ` issue.

3. Line 130 in pennylane/transforms/control.py introduces `ops` which is not used anywhere and leads to an `unused-variable` issue. 

**Description of the Change:**

To fix issues 1 and 2, `pylint:disable=arguments-differ` is added to both files similar to what we have [here](https://github.com/PennyLaneAI/pennylane/blob/23b82a4d6b7c5a42d2a4a9e660ac7f61f2919e29/pennylane/ops/qubit/parametric_ops.py#L18).

author: ludoboludo
body:
**Why are these changes introduced?**

Fixes an issue where the previous button on the slideshow is disabled. It doesn't come up when you first add the section in the editor but does once you've saved. 

Didn't notice it before, so I'm wondering what could potentially have triggered it 🤔  Seems like an issue with the order in which functions/values are being called. 

I think it's due to the fact that the slideshow component is extending the slider component and has a different value for `this.enableSliderLooping`. But when it runs `update()` it's using the `false` value set in `sliderComponent` first which disables the previous button and only after that it notices the different value set within the slideshow component.

**What approach did you take?**

I added a check in the `update()` within the slideshow component. So that if it sees the `disabled` attribute it removes it.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/17108460/146440372-84329b73-4d36-4a61-873a-0e0d37730459.png)

* Allows to generate ellipses by passing `width` and `height`.
* Accuracy is much better for thin shapes. The circle shape can be scaled (see bottom shape), but this degrades accuracy. Using an ellipse shape is efficient in this regard because you don't have to make `max_error` extremely low to achieve the same accuracy that would lead to performance loss during boolean operations between other `PolyNode2D`-based shapes.

author: tsibley
body:
This will alleviate somewhat the rate limits imposed on unauthenticated
requests.  As of this writing, authenticated requests get 5,000
requests/hour per authenticated user (_not_ per token).  Unauthenticated
requests get only 60 requests/hour per IP.¹

Resolves #93.

Other future changes to address rate limiting might include switching
from simple fetch()es to an API client that does dynamic throttling to
respect the rate limits.  Octokit does a great job of making this easy,
for example.²  Complications with using Octokit include figuring out how
to incorporate our current caching, or an equivalent. Caching is an
important part of reducing these requests.  Another complication is how
long to retry before returning a 500 error to the nextstrain.org
request; the example above retries indefinitely, but that's likely not
what we want for nextstrain.org.

¹ https://docs.github.com/en/rest/overview/resources-in-the-rest-api#rate-limiting
² https://github.com/nextstrain/community-search/blob/ce1a4146878e8336c442a175033ad242621f5a17/find#L2-L25

author: marioevz
body:
This PR adds a new simulator ethereum/engine which tests the new merge Engine API by the use of a mocking tool which mimics the Consensus Layer in order to send testing API calls to the Execution Clients.

The simulator at the moment depends on MariusVanDerWijden/go-ethereum@merge-devnet-3 due to required structures to format the Engine API calls in "github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/eth/catalyst", which are unavailable on the master branch.
In the case that this is not acceptable, it can be sorted out by simply copying the definitions into engineclient.go in this PR.

Currently, none of the clients will succeed in running the Engine API tests since this functionality is not included in the master branches of the clients, but the simulator can be used for local testing of the clients with the appropriate modifications to each of the clients' Dockerfile.

A full description of the simulator, along with the test cases currently implemented, is included in the Readme file.

```

notAfter=Nov 13 14:38:20 2031 GMT

body:
This PR removes the default styling from the standard dialog modal and adds support for some modal style properties: background/backdrop color, corner radius, border (radius/color), shadow.

One interesting nuance is because this border is applied by UIKit, it's positioned differently from the SwiftUI ones. A 10px border in a 200px wide view in UIKit leaves 180px of space in the box, where SwiftUI would leave 190px because the center of the border is the edge of the view. We may want to normalize this at some point in the future.

Margin/padding support will be a separate PR.

For bonus points we could try to be really smart about positioning the skip button for really large corner radius values... 🤔

author: worldsender
body:
#### Description

Fixes #2206

This is in some sense a very poor-mans local fix. It works and has a test case - good.

There is something deeper to fix: every `NodeRef` should be owned by exactly one rendered vnode. If that invariant is violated, this could lead to unexpected results - like here: Complicating the situation is that during rendering, new nodes are mounted and refs are set immediately, while another part of nodes might get detached later during the same render - "owning" the same ref - leading to a time window where a `NodeRef` is "owned" by two nodes.

There might be other, similar bugs lying dormant until a bigger effort is spent on developing a conceptual understanding of the above and adding some more debug assertions to check for the implicit invariant. Note that for example, there are currently no checks for the user reusing the same `NodeRef` multiple times:

```
<>
  <div ref={&some_ref} />
  <div ref={&some_ref} />
</>
```

Which of those divs is expected to be in `some_ref`? Imo, some `debug_assertion` should trigger and inform the user not to do this in debug builds.

author: cosama
body:
This will fix an issue I have been observing for a while now but had a hard time to figure out how to deal with it. Up to now when the driver was run at more than maybe 80Hz or so, then packages didn't arrive at well defined intervals. The packages will still be published at the right rate, but a few of them will have header.stamps really close in time, followed by a larger gap.

I talked to the guys over at vectornav and this was the solution we came up with to address it to some extent. I am not sure if they will be adding this to their driver (where it would be easier to implement), so I added a little hack here that does the same. This should also be achieved by using the command line and type either:


```
setserial /dev/<tty_name> low_latency
```

or

```
echo 1 > /sys/bus/usb-serial/devices/<tty_name>/latency_timer
```

However, I think the in program solution is more elegant. This will only affect operation on linux. I have not tested this anywhere else, and it should not enable the function on another system. The changes to the serial port will stay effective after the first call until the cable is unplugged.

I also made sure that output register 2 and 3 won't publish any data, when running this driver. Furthermore, I removed a line from the INSGROUP that the vectornav representative pointed out to be identical to COMMONGROUP_POSITION and thus not necessary.

author: teogeb
body:
Updated CLI-tools to use latest `StreamrClient`. Refactored most of the commands to use new `createClientCommand` helper method, which handles the initialization of `StreamrClient`, and destroying the instance when the command completes.

Updated `commander` dependency to 8.3.0. The functionality of `exitWithHelpIfArgsNotBetween` is now implemented with `allowExcessArguments(false)`.

Divided the three resend commands to separate files, similarly to other commands. Inlined some command-specific helper functions from `src` folder to the command files.

### Configuration management

It is now possible to specify a configuration file with `--config` argument. All `StreamrClient` options can be configured in that file (the format of the file is same as `StreamrClient` constructor options). If no configuration file is specified, default options are read from `~/.streamr/config/default.json`. 

The config file format is also compatible with Broker config format. The configuration file must contain `client` block as a root level element, and additional fields are allowed so that a Broker config file passes the validation.

Removed `--http-url` and `--ws-url` argument which are no longer supported by the client. Dropped also `--stg` argument, but we can add that later when new configuration values for the staging environment are available. The `--dev` and `--privateKey` arguments are still supported.

### Other changes related to StreamrClient v6 update

Updated permission handling:
- enum values: `share` is now `grant`, `get` is removed
- `stream grant-permission`: dropped support for legacy enum names like 'stream_get`
- `stream revoke-permission`: references permissions by user, not by `permissionId`
- `stream list --permission`: modified to use the same enums as other commands

Removed two columns from `stream list` output:
- `lastUpdated` (not supported)
- `name` (deprecated)

Relative streamIds are supported natively by `StreamrClient`. There is no longer need to do that transformation in the CLI-tools.

### Future improvements

- When Broker's Config Wizard generates a new config file, it could use  `~/.streamr/config/default.json` as default location.

body:
Tpu::new() now matches Tvu::new() in having struct to reduce argument
list. Additionally, Rust supports partial moves, so there is no need to
clone the Tvu sockets out of Node object.

This struct is purely to reduce the argument list down. We clearly exceed the "recommended" number of arguments in `Tpu::new()` & `Tvu::new()` argument lists; however, I'd argue the two should be consistent. So, if someone doesn't like the addition of a cosmetic struct like this, I'd contend that we should rip the existing struct out of `Tvu::new()`.

Regardless of where we land on structs, we can definitely take advantage of partial move to not have to copy the Tvu sockets out of `Node`.
https://doc.rust-lang.org/rust-by-example/scope/move/partial_move.html

The pattern used for flattening is ```<type>__<FHIR field name>__<system>```, where:
- ```type``` can be:
  - ```code``` for codable concepts
  - ```ex``` for extensions
  - ```identifier``` for identifiers
- if ```type``` and ```FHIR field name``` are the same, ```<type>__``` is dropped (for example, we don't want ```identifier__identifier__NPI```)
- if there is only 1 system for the field, ```__<system>``` can be dropped

author: jaylim-crl
body:
Fixes https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/issues/69220.
Regression from https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/pull/67452.

In #67452, we omitted DRAINING pods from the tenant directory. Whenever a pod
goes into the DRAINING state, the pod watcher needs time to update the
directory. Not waiting for that while calling EnsureTenantAddr produces a
stale result. This commit updates TestWatchPods by polling on EnsureTenantAddr
until the pod watcher updates the directory.

Another high-severity CVE was found in `armeria` so I upgraded from `1.13.2` to `1.13.4`.

I added `dependency-check-maven` to the root POM so that dependencies all modules will be checked for CVE's.  When doing a build, the check will run during the `verify` phase, and the aggregate report will be written to `target/dependency-check-report.html`.

The dependency check plugin has an option to fail the build if any high-severity CVE's are found.  I decided to turn that option off as I believe it will make the build too brittle.  This means that a manual review of `target/dependency-check-report.html` is required to see if any vulnerabilities are present.

The report currently shows high-severity CVS's in `karate-gatling`, `karate-demo`, and `karate-robot`.  While it would be nice to address those in the future, I believe we can leave them for now since those modules are not shaded.
